title: Root cause report: fanout-induced queue backpressure and autoscaler contention (customer SLO misses)
content:
Summary:

Between 2025-07-14 22:10 UTC and 2025-07-15 02:45 UTC several customers reported SLO misses (95th pct latency spikes) for hosted-generation endpoints. The spike correlated with an internal rollout of a multi-hop fanout feature used by a small set of customers (fanout size up to 6), which increased concurrent in-flight subrequests per top-level request. The serving runtime began to exhibit long tail latency due to queue backpressure and autoscaler contention on a subset of GPU nodes.

Impact:
- Affected customers: 3 high-volume hosted API customers (reported via support; RM-1284).
- Observed SLO violations: 95th percentile token latency rose from ~120ms to ~650ms for affected endpoints.
- Duration: active degradation first observed ~2025-07-14 22:10 UTC; mitigations rolled out and stable by ~2025-07-15 03:10 UTC.
- User-visible symptoms: prolonged streaming delays and occasional dropped connections in high-fanout requests.

High-level timeline (UTC):
- 22:05: Canary rollout of fanout v2 (gradual) begins for 2% traffic.
- 22:10: Monitoring alerts: generation-95th latency breaches threshold for region us-west1.
- 22:12: Support ticket RM-1284 created; first customer report.
- 22:20: Pager on-call (Jordi) begins triage; initial hypothesis: model change or token-length tail.
- 22:40: Profiling snapshots taken from impacted nodes (flamegraphs, grpc queue metrics).
- 23:00: Hotfix #1: reduce fanout cap from 6 -> 3 via API-gateway feature flag (rollback-able).
- 23:25: Partial improvement; 95th latency drops but still above SLO.
- 00:05: Hotfix #2: raise per-worker gRPC inflight queue limit and disable autoscaler downscaling for 10m window.
- 00:35: Latency returns to near-normal for most traffic; continued monitoring overnight.
- 03:10: Incident declared mitigated; post-incident investigation started.

Investigation details and evidence:
1) Request pattern analysis:
- Fanout v2 increased median subrequest count per top-level request from 1 -> 2.8 and 99th from 3 -> 6. This multiplied the number of concurrent KV-cache contexts and active CUDA streams on a worker.
- Tokens per top-level request did not change substantially; problem is concurrency amplification.

2) Observed node-level signals (collected via perf-collector and eBPF traces):
- gRPC inbound queue length spiked to >1200 on a small subset of nodes (normal <100).
- Kernel-level runqueue intermittently saturated during high-fanout bursts (coincident with memcpy bursts).
- GPU utilization remained high (~85-95%) but did not explain 5x tail latency; instead we saw long queueing in the runtime scheduler.

3) Runtime profiling and flamegraphs:
- Continuous-batching scheduler showed increased wait time in schedule_next_batch() path; batch formation delays increased the per-token latency for tail requests.
- KV cache lock contention increased: high-fanout access patterns produced frequent concurrent KV cache insertions causing short mutex holds but many waits at 99.9th pct.
- Memory copy hotspots: repeated small host->device memcpy calls were observed due to many small subrequests rather than fewer larger ones. Aggregated overhead of these calls increased tail latency.

4) Autoscaler interactions:
- Horizontal autoscaler configured with reactive policy: scale-down threshold at 60s idle. Under heavy fanout bursts, autoscaler tried to downscale some nodes between bursts; but because fanout multiplies concurrency, cold nodes that were brought back up saw slower warmup (GPU context re-initialization + cache coldness), worsening tail latency.
- There was a brief race where autoscaler and scheduler both tried to shift load causing temporary overcommit on remaining nodes.

Root cause (summary):
- The fanout change amplified request-level concurrency leading to: increased runtime scheduler queueing, KV cache contention, a higher rate of small host->device memcpy calls, and stress on autoscaler lifecycle (downscale/scale-up race). Combined, these produced long-tail latency spikes at the 95/99 percentiles for affected endpoints.

Immediate mitigations and hotfix validation:
- Hotfix 1: cap fanout at 3 for gradual rollout customers (feature flag). Verified by toggling flag in staging and observing request concurrency metrics drop.
- Hotfix 2: temporarily raised per-worker gRPC inflight queue limit from 256 -> 512 and disabled scale-down for affected pools for 15 minutes. This reduced recovery churn and allowed KV caches to persist between bursts.
- Hotfix 3 (follow-up): batching heuristic change to prefer combining small subrequests arriving within 10ms window into one larger batch when compatible; deployment of heuristic A/B tested in canary reduced memcpy call count by ~38%.

Validation checks performed after mitigations (evidence):
- Canary traffic with fanout=3: 95th latency returned to baseline within 20 minutes in us-west1.
- Profiling snapshots post-hotfix show schedule_next_batch wait time dropped by ~60% at 95th pct.
- KV cache mutex contention reduced (99.9th wait times down by ~4.3x).
- No dropped connections or client errors reported after 00:40 UTC.

Customer communication:
- Support sent initial acknowledgment at 22:25 UTC and set expectations.
- Follow-up status update at 01:15 UTC indicated hotfixes in flight.
- Post-incident email to affected customers drafted and approved (RM-1284). Draft includes explanation, mitigations taken, and timeline.

Action items (owner assignments):
- Short term (<=2 weeks):
  - Implement a permanent fanout-safe batching pathway that coalesces small subrequests when source prompt compatibility allows (Samir).
  - Adjust autoscaler policy: increase idle threshold and add hysteresis to avoid downscale during high-variance workloads (Jordi + SRE).
  - Tune per-worker inflight limits more conservatively and add adaptive limit based on observed node pressure (Maya).
- Medium term (<=2 months):
  - Rework KV cache locking to reduce global contention: explore sharded locks or lock-free insertion path (Lena + Eng-APPLIED-ML).
  - Add end-to-end chaos tests that simulate fanout multipliers and autoscaler churn in staging (Eng-Release).
  - Add tenant-level circuit breaker to limit fanout multiplier dynamically when node pressure detected (Product + Runtime).

Open tickets and tracking:
- RM-1284: customer-facing communication and closure (priority P1).
- RM-1290: batching heuristic implementation and tests.
- RM-1291: autoscaler policy change RFC and rollout plan.
- GH PR 678: temporary inflight queue limit bump and feature-flag for fanout cap.

Lessons learned / notes:
- Increasing request fanout is a multiplicative change surface area: even modest per-request subreq increases can overwhelm downstream runtime assumptions. Need a checklist before shipping fanout-style features that touches runtime and autoscaler teams.
- Observability gaps: we lacked a direct metric that multiplies concurrent subrequests per top-level request; adding a top-level request fanout histogram would have shortened MTTI.
- Autoscaler hysteresis should be workload-aware rather than strictly idle-time based.

Appendix (commands / snippets used during investigation):
- Collecting flamegraph on node-123: sudo perf record -F 99 -g -p $(pgrep serving-runtime) -- sleep 30; sudo perf script | flamegraph.pl > /tmp/flame.svg
- KV cache lock blocker query (example): sudo ebpf-trace --pid $(pgrep serving-runtime) -c 'probe:block_time("kv_cache_lock")' --duration 60s
- Quick metric checks:
  - kubectl -n runtime get hpa,deployments --selector=pool=gen-us-west1
  - influxdb query: SELECT percentile("latency_ms", 95) FROM "generation" WHERE region='us-west1' AND time > '2025-07-14T22:00:00Z'

Contact for follow-up: Maya Chen (owner) — maya@redwood.ai, #eng-serving-runtime on Slack.

Document history: created 2025-07-16 by Maya Chen; triage notes added 2025-07-17 to 2025-07-22 by collaborators; final validation snapshot attached 2025-07-23.
